turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The article is called 'The Last 50%.' What is that referring to?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: AI handles the first half well: structure, outline, rough pass. The last 50%, where trust actually lives, is specificity, originality, and editorial judgment. That part can't be delegated, and skipping it is the actual failure.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: But hasn't Google been cracking down on AI-generated content?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: That's the misread. Google never penalized AI content specifically. It ranked it the same way it always ranked everything: does it demonstrate real experience and expertise? The penalty is a reader penalty, not an algorithm penalty. Edelman's 2025 study found 73% of consumers can spot AI slop, and 61% say it lowers their trust in the source.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: 'AI slop' was literally the American Dialect Society's Word of the Year in 2025. What makes something slop versus legitimate AI-assisted writing?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Not the tool used. Slop is a specific failure pattern: no point of view, structural padding substituted for substance, generic phrasing that could have come from any source, and nothing that proves someone actually did the thing being written about. It's the cluster that signals it, not any single word.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The article lists specific verbal tells. What are the patterns that give it away?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Four clusters: throat-clearing openers like 'In today's fast-paced world,' hedge-stacking phrases like 'can potentially' and 'it's worth noting that,' empty transitions like 'that being said' and 'moving forward,' and inflated vocabulary like 'delve,' 'elevate,' 'robust,' 'seamless' used in place of an actual claim.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So what does the six-step fix actually start with?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Start with your own voice before opening the prompt box. Record yourself talking through the idea, or write an unstructured brain dump first. That raw material is what keeps the eventual piece from starting life as a generic take on the topic.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And then AI comes in?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: At step two: outlines, H2 and H3 scaffolding, topic-cluster brainstorming, turning a long document into a summary, expanding a keyword list. That's where AI is genuinely strongest and where it saves real time. Step three is writing or heavily rewriting the actual sentences yourself.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the single most effective thing a writer can add to defeat the slop read?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: One detail only they could know. A specific result, an actual number, an opinion they're willing to defend, a first-hand observation. That single move does more to defeat both slop-perception and algorithmic demotion than any amount of line-editing.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The article treats fact-checking AI contributions as serious. How serious?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Treat every AI-sourced fact as unverified until you've checked it yourself. Hallucinated statistics and fabricated citations are a normal failure mode, not an edge case. Citing a made-up number while writing about trust is the kind of thing that ends reputations.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's E-E-A-T, and why does it keep coming up here?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Google's quality framework: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness. The four components collapse to one practical question: does this content contain something that could only have come from actually doing the thing? Generic best-practices content, however well-structured, is exactly what E-E-A-T is designed to rank below something narrower but real.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The article ends with 'the writing is the thinking.' Is there a practical test for whether you've done the thinking?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Before publishing, read it aloud once. Clichéd AI-pattern phrasing is far more audible than it is visible on a screen. Cut anything that sounds like it's clearing its throat before saying something. And check: does any sentence survive purely because it sounds good? If yes, delete it. Length that isn't earning its place is the single most common slop signal.
